title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 127 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 605–607 (Night 127, continuing directly from nights-126), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 127 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. Cast out maimed at the garden gate, he makes his way home to find his father dead and his mother weeping for him. Now he knows how much his dead cousin ʿAzīza loved him. When he has healed, his mother gives him what ʿAzīza left in her keeping: the cloth with the gazelle, inscribed with a lament in verse, and a last letter that forgives him her death and asks him to keep the cloth always. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-seventh night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِلْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشَّابَّ عَزِيزًا قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ ثُمَّ إِنِّي لَمَّا قُمْتُ وَصَحَوْتُ وَجَدْتُ نَفْسِي مُلْقًى عَلَى بَابِ الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni thumma inna al-shābba ʿazīzan qāla li-tāji al-mulūki thumma innī lammā qumtu wa-ṣaḥawtu wajadtu nafsī mulqan ʿalā bābi al-bustāni
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to the king Ḍawʾ al-Makān: Then the young-man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: Then I, when I rose and woke, found my soul cast-down at the door of the garden.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān told King Ḍawʾ al-Makān that the young man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: When I got up and came to myself, I found myself lying cast out at the garden gate.
sentences.n: The print has تاج الملك, a misprint for تاج الملوك (Tāj al-Mulūk, the name the tale gives him throughout), corrected here. The night opens, as the nights often do, by repeating where the last one stopped: ʿAzīz waking at the garden gate after the lady has mutilated him. li-al-maliki, “to the king”: Ḍawʾ al-Makān is now king, and Dandān’s story is told to him. mulqan, “thrown down, cast aside”, the passive participle of alqā.

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ وَأَنَا أَئِنُّ وَأَتَضَجَّرُ وَتَمَشَّيْتُ حَتَّى أَتَيْتُ إِلَى مَنْزِلِي فَدَخَلْتُ فِيهِ فَوَجَدْتُ أُمِّي تَبْكِي عَلَيَّ وَتَقُولُ يَاهَلْ تُرَي يَاوَلَدِي أَنْتَ فِي أَيِّ أَرْضٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu wa-anā aʾinnu wa-ataḍajjaru wa-tamashshaytu ḥattā ataytu ilā manzilī fa-dakhaltu fīhi fa-wajadtu ummī tabkī ʿalayya wa-taqūlu yā hal turā yā waladī anta fī ayyi arḍin
sentences.l: And I rose, and I groaning and fretting, and I walked until I came to my dwelling; and I entered into it and found my mother weeping over me and saying: O, is it seen, O my son, (that) you (are) in which land?
sentences.i: I got up, groaning and fretting, and walked until I reached my house. I went in and found my mother weeping for me and saying, “Ah, my son, I wonder in what land you are now!”
sentences.n: The print marks the kasra and shadda in aʾinnu, “I groan”, and on ʿalayya. ataḍajjaru, “I fret, I chafe”. yā hal turā, “O, is it to be seen …?”: the stock spoken opener of a wondering question, “I wonder”; the print writes turā with final yāʾ (تري), as it often writes ى as ي, and runs yā into hal and into waladī.

sentences.t: فَدَنَوْتُ مِنْهَا وَرَمَيْتُ نَفْسِي عَلَيْهَا فَلَمَّا نَظَرَتْ إِلَيَّ وَحَسَّتْ بِي وَجَدَتْنِي عَلَى غَيْرِ اسْتِوَأٍ وَصَارَ عَلَى وَجْهِي الِاصْفِرَارُ وَالسَّوَادُ
sentences.tr: fa-danawtu minhā wa-ramaytu nafsī ʿalayhā fa-lammā naẓarat ilayya wa-ḥassat bī wajadatnī ʿalā ghayri istiwāʾin wa-ṣāra ʿalā wajhī al-iṣfirāru wa-al-sawādu
sentences.l: And I drew-near to her and threw my soul upon her; and when she looked at me and felt me, she found me upon other-than evenness, and there had come upon my face the yellowness and the blackness.
sentences.i: I went up to her and threw myself into her arms. When she looked at me and felt me, she found me not as I should be: my face had turned yellow and dark.
sentences.n: ḥassat bī, “she felt me, sensed me”: the spoken ḥassa bi- for classical aḥassa bi-. ʿalā ghayri istiwāʾin, “not in a sound state”: the print spells istiwāʾ with the hamza set over a final alif (استوأ) instead of after it; the word is not in doubt and the print’s spelling is kept. The yellow and dark face is the pallor of a man who has lost much blood.

sentences.t: فَتَفَكَّرْتُ بِنْتَ عَمِّي وَمَافَعَلَتْ مَعِي مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَتَحَقَّقْتُ أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تُحِبُّنِي فَبَكَيْتُ عَلَيْهَا وَبَكَتْ أُمِّي
sentences.tr: fa-tafakkartu binta ʿammī wa-mā faʿalat maʿī mina al-maʿrūfi wa-taḥaqqaqtu annahā kānat tuḥibbunī fa-bakaytu ʿalayhā wa-bakat ummī
sentences.l: And I recalled the daughter of my uncle and what she had done with me of the kindness, and I made-certain that she had been loving me; and I wept over her, and my mother wept.
sentences.i: Then I thought of my cousin and all the kindness she had shown me, and I knew for certain that she had loved me; and I wept for her, and my mother wept too.
sentences.n: tafakkara takes its object directly here, “to call to mind”. The print runs mā into faʿalat (مافعلت), and marks the shadda in tuḥibbunī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ أُمِّي يَاوَلَدِي إِنَّ وَالِدَكَ قَدْمَاتَ فَازْدَدْتُ غَيْظًا وَبَكَيْتُ حَتَّى أُغْمِيَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ummī yā waladī inna wālidaka qad māta fa-izdadtu ghayẓan wa-bakaytu ḥattā ughmiya ʿalayya
sentences.l: And my mother said: O my son, your father has died. And I increased (in) rage, and wept until it was swooned upon me.
sentences.i: Then my mother said, “My son, your father is dead.” At that my anguish grew, and I wept until I fainted.
sentences.n: qad māta: the print runs qad into the verb (قدمات). ghayẓ is properly “rage”, here the bitterness of grief upon grief. ughmiya ʿalayya, “it was swooned upon me”: the impersonal passive that Arabic uses for fainting.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَقْتُ نَظَرْتُ إِلَى مَوْضِعِ ابْنَةِ عَمِّي الَّتِي كَانَتْ تَقْعُدُ فِيهِ فَبَكَيْتُ ثَانِيًا وَكِدْتُ أَنْ أُغْمِيَ عَلَيَّ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْبُكَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afaqtu naẓartu ilā mawḍiʿi ibnati ʿammī allatī kānat taqʿudu fīhi fa-bakaytu thāniyan wa-kidtu an ughmiya ʿalayya min shiddati al-bukāʾi
sentences.l: And when I came-to, I looked at the place of the daughter of my uncle which she used to sit in, and I wept a second (time), and I almost — that it was swooned upon me from the vehemence of the weeping.
sentences.i: When I came to, I looked at the place where my cousin used to sit, and I wept again, and almost fainted a second time from the violence of my weeping.
sentences.n: kidtu an ughmiya ʿalayya, “I nearly fainted”: the print has the perfect ughmiya after an, where Classical grammar, after kāda, wants an imperfect; it is vocalised as printed. The relative clause allatī kānat taqʿudu fīhi points back to the place, mawḍiʿ, through fīhi, “in it”.

sentences.t: وَمَازِلْتُ فِي هَذَاالْبُكَاءِ وَالنَّحِيبِ إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā ziltu fī hādhā al-bukāʾi wa-al-naḥībi ilā niṣfi al-layli
sentences.l: And I did not cease in this the weeping and the sobbing until the half of the night.
sentences.i: And I went on weeping and sobbing until midnight.
sentences.n: mā ziltu fī, “I kept on in”. The print runs hādhā into al-bukāʾ (هذاالبكاء).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي أُمِّي إِنَّ لِوَالِدِكَ عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَهُوَمَيِّتٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī ummī inna li-wālidika ʿasharata ayyāmin wa-huwa mayyitun
sentences.l: And my mother said to me: To your father (are) ten days and he dead.
sentences.i: Then my mother said to me, “Your father has been dead ten days.”
sentences.n: inna li-wālidika ʿasharata ayyāmin wa-huwa mayyitun, “your father has ten days, and he dead”: li-, “to, for”, marks the one whose time it is, and the circumstantial wa-huwa says in what state — the spoken way of saying how long something has been so. The print runs huwa into mayyit (وهوميت).

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا إِنِّي لَا أُفَكِّرُ فِي أَحَدٍ أَبَدًا غَيْرَ ابْنَةِ عَمِّي لِأَنِّي أَسْتَحِقُّ كُلَّ مَاحَصَلَ لِي حَيْثُ أَهْمَلْتُهَا وَهِيَ تُحِبُّنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā innī lā ufakkiru fī aḥadin abadan ghayra ibnati ʿammī li-annī astaḥiqqu kulla mā ḥaṣala lī ḥaythu ahmaltuhā wa-hiya tuḥibbunī
sentences.l: And I said to her: I do not think about anyone ever other-than the daughter of my uncle, because I deserve all that has befallen me, since I neglected her and she loving me.
sentences.i: I said to her, “I can think of no one but my cousin, for I deserve everything that has happened to me: I neglected her, and she loved me.”
sentences.n: ḥaythu, “where”, is used in the spoken sense “since, seeing that”. li-annī, “because I”. The print runs mā into ḥaṣala (ماحصل) here and in the next sentence.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَمَاحَصَلَ لَكَ فَحَكَيْتُ لَهَا مَاحَصَلَ لِي فَبَكَتْ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَأَحْضَرَتْ لِي شَيْأً مِنَ الْمَأْكُولِ فَأَكَلْتُ قَلِيلًا وَشَرِبْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-mā ḥaṣala laka fa-ḥakaytu lahā mā ḥaṣala lī fa-bakat sāʿatan thumma qāmat wa-aḥḍarat lī shayʾan mina al-maʾkūli fa-akaltu qalīlan wa-sharibtu
sentences.l: And she said: And what has befallen you? And I related to her what had befallen me; and she wept an hour, then rose and brought for me a thing of the eaten-stuff, and I ate a little and drank.
sentences.i: “And what has happened to you?” she asked. I told her what had happened to me, and she wept for a while; then she got up and brought me something to eat, and I ate a little and drank.
sentences.n: The print spells shayʾan with the hamza on an alif (شيأ), as it usually does. sāʿatan, “an hour”, is any short while. al-maʾkūl, “what is eaten”, food.

sentences.t: وَأَعَدْتُ لَهَا قِصَّتِي وَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِجَمِيعِ مَا وَقَعَ لِى فَقَالَتِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي جَرَي لَكَ هَذَا وَمَا ذَبَحَتْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿadtu lahā qiṣṣatī wa-akhbartuhā bi-jamīʿi mā waqaʿa lī fa-qālati al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī jarā laka hādhā wa-mā dhabaḥatka
sentences.l: And I repeated to her my story and informed her of all that had happened to me; and she said: The praise (be) to God, that this happened to you and she did not slaughter you!
sentences.i: I told her my story again, and all that had befallen me, and she said, “Praise be to God that this is what befell you, and that she did not cut your throat!”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-: the verb takes bi- for the thing told. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī …: alladhī here does the work of “that”, giving the reason for the praise, a spoken use. The print writes jarā with final yāʾ (جري).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا عَالَجَتْنِي وَدَاوَتْنِي حَتَّى بَرِئْتُ وَتَكَامَلَتْ عَافِيَتِي
sentences.tr: thumma innahā ʿālajatnī wa-dāwatnī ḥattā bariʾtu wa-takāmalat ʿāfiyatī
sentences.l: Then she treated me and doctored me until I was-cured and my health became-complete.
sentences.i: Then she nursed and doctored me until I was healed and my strength had fully returned.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِى يَا وَلَدِي الْآنَ أُخْرِجُ لَكَ الْوَدَاعَةَ الَّتِي وَضَعَتْهَا عِنْدِي بِنْتُ عَمِّكَ فَإِنَّهَا لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī yā waladī al-āna ukhriju laka al-wadāʿata allatī waḍaʿathā ʿindī bintu ʿammika fa-innahā laka
sentences.l: And she said to me: O my son, now I bring-out for you the trust which the daughter of your uncle put with me, for it (is) yours.
sentences.i: Then she said to me, “My son, now I will bring out for you what your cousin left in my keeping, for it is yours.
sentences.n: al-wadāʿa: the print’s word for the thing left in trust. The Classical word is wadīʿa, “a deposit”; wadāʿa properly means “gentleness”. The print’s form is kept.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ حَلَّفَتْنِي أَنِّي لَا أُخْرِجُهَا لَكَ حَتَّى أَرَاكَ تَتَذَكَّرُهَا وَتَبْكِي عَلَيْهَا وَتَنْقَطِعُ عَلَائُقُكَ مِنْ غَيْرِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad ḥallafatnī annī lā ukhrijuhā laka ḥattā arāka tatadhakkaruhā wa-tabkī ʿalayhā wa-tanqaṭiʿu ʿalāʾiquka min ghayrihā
sentences.l: And she had made me swear that I would not bring it out for you until I see you remembering her and weeping over her, and your ties being-cut from (anyone) other-than her.
sentences.i: She made me swear not to give it to you until I saw you remembering her and weeping for her, with every tie to anyone else cut off.
sentences.n: The print has لأ, a misprint for لا (lā, “not”), corrected here: the hamza is a stray mark on the negative. ḥallafatnī annī lā …, “she made me swear that I would not …”: the oath is reported in the first person, as it was sworn. The print sets a ḍamma on the hamza of ʿalāʾiquka, “your attachments”.

sentences.t: وَالْآنَ عَلِمْتُ فِيكَ هَذِهِ الشُّرُوطَ ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَفَتَحَتْ صُنْدُوقًا وَأَخْرَجَتْ مِنْهُ هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةَ الَّتِى فِيهَا صُورَةُ هَذَا الْغَزَالِ الْمُصَوَّرِ وَهِىَ الَّتِي كُنْتُ وَهَبْتُهَا لَهَا أَوَّلًا
sentences.tr: wa-al-āna ʿalimtu fīka hādhihi al-shurūṭa thumma qāmat wa-fataḥat ṣundūqan wa-akhrajat minhu hādhihi al-khirqata allatī fīhā ṣūratu hādhā al-ghazāli al-muṣawwari wa-hiya allatī kuntu wahabtuhā lahā awwalan
sentences.l: And now I have known in you these the conditions. Then she rose and opened a chest and brought out from it this the rag in which (is) the picture of this the gazelle, the pictured; and it (is) the-one which I had given to her at-first.
sentences.i: And now I see these conditions met in you.” Then she got up, opened a chest, and took out of it this piece of cloth with the figure of this gazelle worked on it — the very one I had given her in the first place.
sentences.n: ʿalimtu fīka, “I have come to know in you”: she sees the conditions fulfilled in him. al-khirqa, “the rag, the piece of cloth”: ʿAzīz is holding it as he speaks to Tāj al-Mulūk, hence “this cloth”, “this gazelle”. The print writes allatī and hiya with final ى in two places and marks the shadda in awwalan.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَخَذْتُهَا وَجَدْتُ مَكْتُوبًا فِيهَا هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā akhadhtuhā wajadtu maktūban fīhā hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: And when I took it, I found written in it these the verses:
sentences.i: When I took it, I found these lines written on it:
sentences.n: maktūban, “written”, is the object of wajadtu, and the verses are what is written, so they stand in the nominative.

sentences.t:
يَارَبَّةَ الْحُسْنِ مَنْ بِالصَّدِّ اَغْرَاكِ * حَتَّى قَتَلْتِ بِفَرْطِ الْحُبِّ مُضْنَاكِ
اِنْ كُنْتِ لَمْ تَذْكُرِينَا بَعْدَ فُرْقَتِنَا * فَاللّٰهُ يَعْلَمُ اَنَّا مَا نَسِينَاكِ
عَذَّبْتِنِي بِالتَّجَنِّي وَهْوَ يَعْذُبُ لِي * فَهَلْ تَجُودِينَ لِي يَوْمًا بِرُؤْيَاكِ
مَاكُنْتُ اَحْسِبُ اَنَّ الْحُبَّ فِيهِ ضَنَا * وَلَا عَذَابَ نُفُوسٍ قَبْلَ اَهْوَاكِ
حَتَّى تَوَلَّعَ قَلْبِي بِالْغَرَامِ فَمَا * اَمْسَى اَسِيرَ الْهَوَى فِى لَحْظِ عَيْنَاكِ
رَقَّ الْعَذُولُ لِحَالِي فِي الْهَوَى وَرَثَى * وَاَنْتِ يَا هِنْدُ لَمْ تَرْثِي لِمُضْنَاكِ
تَاللّٰهِ لَوْمُتُّ لَمْ اَسْلُوكِ يَا اَمَلِي * وَلَوْ فَنِيتُ غَرَامًا لَسْتُ اَنْسَاكِ
sentences.tr:
yā rabbata al-ḥusni man bi-al-ṣaddi aghrāki * ḥattā qatalti bi-farṭi al-ḥubbi muḍnāki
in kunti lam tadhkurīnā baʿda furqatinā * fa-allāhu yaʿlamu annā mā nasīnāki
ʿadhdhabtinī bi-al-tajannī wa-hwa yaʿdhubu lī * fa-hal tajūdīna lī yawman bi-ruʾyāki
mā kuntu aḥsibu anna al-ḥubba fīhi ḍanan * wa-lā ʿadhāba nufūsin qabla ahwāki
ḥattā tawallaʿa qalbī bi-al-gharāmi fa-mā * amsā asīra al-hawā fī laḥẓi ʿaynāki
raqqa al-ʿadhūlu li-ḥālī fī al-hawā wa-rathā * wa-anti yā hindu lam tarthī li-muḍnāki
ta-llāhi law muttu lam aslūki yā amalī * wa-law fanītu gharāman lastu ansāki
sentences.l:
O mistress of the beauty, who with the turning-away incited you, * until you killed, with excess of the love, the-one-you-wasted?
If you have not remembered us after our parting, * then God knows that we have not forgotten you.
You tormented me with the false-blaming, and it is sweet to me; * so will you be-generous to me one day with your sight?
I did not reckon that the love, in it (is) wasting, * nor torment of souls, before I loved you,
until my heart became-enamoured with the passion, and so * it became a captive of the love in the glance of your eyes.
The blamer softened for my state in the love and pitied, * and you, O Hind, did not pity the-one-you-wasted.
By God, if I died I would not be-consoled for you, O my hope, * and if I perished of passion, I would not forget you.
sentences.i:
Lady of beauty, who taught you to turn away, * till with too much love you killed the one you wore away?
If you have not remembered us since we parted, * God knows that we have not forgotten you.
You tormented me with false reproaches, and they are sweet to me; * will you not grant me one day the sight of you?
I never thought that love held wasting sickness, * or torment of the soul, before I loved you,
till my heart was smitten with passion, and so * it became love’s captive in the glances of your eyes.
Even my censor was moved by my plight in love and pitied me, * but you, O Hind, had no pity for the one you wore away.
By God, though I die I will not cease to long for you, my hope; * though passion wastes me away, I will not forget you.
sentences.n: The print points this verse, and it is copied as printed. muḍnāki, “the one you have wasted”, the lover worn thin by love. al-tajannī, “accusing falsely”, the beloved’s trumped-up complaints. qabla ahwāki, “before I loved you”: ahwā is the imperfect of hawiya, and qabla before a bare imperfect is loose verse grammar. fī laḥẓi ʿaynāki: after fī the grammar wants ʿaynayki; the print has the nominative dual ʿaynāki, for the rhyme. Hind is the conventional name of the beloved in Arabic love poetry. The print runs mā into kuntu and law into muttu, and writes lam tarthī and lam aslūki with their long vowels kept after lam, where Classical grammar shortens them. fa-mā amsā (line 5): the mā is hard to place. It is taken here as a filler, “and so it became”; read as a negative it would contradict the line.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأْتُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ بَكَيْتُ بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَلَطَمْتُ عَلَى وَجْهِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾtu hādhihi al-abyāta bakaytu bukāʾan shadīdan wa-laṭamtu ʿalā wajhī
sentences.l: And when I read these the verses, I wept a weeping, a violent (one), and I slapped on my face.
sentences.i: When I read these lines, I wept bitterly and beat my face.
sentences.n: laṭama ʿalā wajhihi, “to slap one’s face”, the gesture of mourning.

sentences.t: وَفَتَحْتُ الرُّقْعَةَ فَوَقَعَتْ مِنْهَا وَرَقَةٌ أُخْرَى فَفَتَحْتُهَا فَإِذَا مَكْتُوبٌ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-fataḥtu al-ruqʿata fa-waqaʿat minhā waraqatun ukhrā fa-fataḥtuhā fa-idhā maktūbun fīhā
sentences.l: And I opened the patch, and there fell from it another leaf; and I opened it, and behold, written in it:
sentences.i: I unfolded the cloth, and another sheet of paper fell out of it. I opened it, and there was written on it:
sentences.n: al-ruqʿa, “the patch, the piece”, is the same cloth, now unfolded. fa-idhā, “and behold”, the idhā of surprise: what he finds is what follows.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي أَنِّي جَعَلْتُكَ فِي حِلٍّ مِنْ دَمِي وَأَرْجُواللَّهَ أَنْ يُوَفِّقَ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ مَنْ تُحِبُّ
sentences.tr: iʿlam yā bna ʿammī annī jaʿaltuka fī ḥillin min damī wa-arjū allāha an yuwaffiqa baynaka wa-bayna man tuḥibbu
sentences.l: Know, O son of my uncle, that I have made you in release from my blood, and I hope God that He will bring-together between you and between whom you love;
sentences.i: “Know, cousin, that I have released you from all guilt for my blood, and I pray God to bring you together with the one you love.
sentences.n: jaʿaltuka fī ḥillin min damī, “I have put you in a state of release from my blood”: she will not hold him answerable for her death, here or at the Judgement. The print marks the shadda in ḥill and runs arjū into allāha (وارجوالله).

sentences.t: لَكِنْ إِذَا أَصَابَكَ شَيْءٌ مِنْ بِنْتِ الدَّلِيلَةِ الْمُحْتَالَةِ فَلَا تَرْجِعْ تَرُوحُ إِلَيْهَا وَلَا لِغَيْرِهَا وَاصْبِرْ عَلَى بَلِيَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: lākin idhā aṣābaka shayʾun min binti al-dalīlati al-muḥtālati fa-lā tarjiʿ tarūḥu ilayhā wa-lā li-ghayrihā wa-iṣbir ʿalā baliyyatika
sentences.l: but if a thing befalls you from the daughter of the Dalīla, the trickster, then do not return going to her, nor to other-than her, and be-patient upon your affliction.
sentences.i: But if any harm comes to you from the daughter of Dalīla the trickster, do not go back to her again, nor to any other woman, but bear your affliction patiently.
sentences.n: bint al-Dalīla al-muḥtāla, “the daughter of Dalīla the trickster”: the name the lady has already had in this tale, after the famous swindling old woman. lā tarjiʿ tarūḥu, “do not go back going”: the spoken use of rajaʿa before a second verb for “to do again”. li-ghayrihā, “to another than her”: li- here, like ilā, marks where he goes. ʿAzīza wrote this before her death, foreseeing what the lady would do.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا أَجَلُكَ مَدِيدٌ لَكُنْتَ هَلَكْتَ مِنْ زَمَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā ajaluka madīdun la-kunta halakta min zamānin
sentences.l: And were-it-not (that) your term (is) long, you would have perished from a time (ago).
sentences.i: Had your appointed time not been long, you would have perished long ago.
sentences.n: lawlā ajaluka madīdun: after lawlā Classical grammar leaves the predicate unspoken; the print supplies it, madīd, “long, drawn out”, as the spoken language does. ajal is the term of a life set by God. min zamānin, “long since”.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي جَعَلَ يَوْمِي قَبْلَ يَوْمِكَ وَسَلَامِي عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākini al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī jaʿala yawmī qabla yawmika wa-salāmī ʿalayka
sentences.l: But the praise (be) to God who made my day before your day; and my peace (be) upon you.
sentences.i: But praise be to God, who set my day before yours. My peace be upon you.
sentences.n: yawmī, “my day”, the day of her death: she thanks God that she died before him and did not see him die. wa-salāmī ʿalayka, “my peace upon you”, the closing of a letter.

sentences.t: وَاحْتَفِظْ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةِ الَّتِي فِيهَا صُورَةُ الْغَزَالِ وَلَا تُخَلِّيهَا تُفَارِقُكَ فَإِنَّ تِلْكَ الصُّورَةَ كَانَتْ تُؤَانِسُنِي إِذَ اغِبْتَ عَنِّى
sentences.tr: wa-iḥtafiẓ ʿalā hādhihi al-khirqati allatī fīhā ṣūratu al-ghazāli wa-lā tukhallīhā tufāriquka fa-inna tilka al-ṣūrata kānat tuʾānisunī idhā ghibta ʿannī
sentences.l: And keep-guard on this the rag in which (is) the picture of the gazelle, and do not let it leave you; for that the picture used to keep me company when you were absent from me.
sentences.i: Take good care of this cloth with the gazelle on it, and do not let it leave you, for that picture kept me company whenever you were away from me.”
sentences.n: iḥtafiẓ ʿalā, “guard, keep safe”, with ʿalā in the spoken way. lā tukhallīhā tufāriquka, “do not let it leave you”: spoken khallā, “to let”, with a second verb, and the long ī kept in the jussive. idhā ghibta, “when you were away”: the print sets the space one letter early, اذ اغبت, so that idhā loses its final alif to ghibta; the reading is not in doubt, and the print’s spacing is kept. The print marks the shadda in ʿannī and writes it with final ى.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
